speechtext:
The House will recall
that at the last sitting a newspaper report was brought to its attention by the right hon. the Prime Minister, in consequence of which I despatched the following telegram yesterday afternoon:	.
June. 14th, 1920.
Rev. Dr. Speer,
Toronto, Ont.
You are reported in a despatch from Toronto which appears in the Ottawa Citizen, newspaper of this date as follows.
* ' Rev. Dr. Speer stated that letters were of no avail in this case, hut money in the lobby. We hadn't the money. I hope the department did something. It was a foregone conclusion that these men of the race track would get what they wanted.'
Kindly inform me whether you made such a statement or one similar in character. If report incorrect I deem it my duty to request you to inform me what you did say concerning this subject. Matter brought to my formal attention in the House to-day by the Prime Minister supported by the leader of the Opposition. An immediate reply is therefore essential.
Edgar N. Rhodes.
Speaker of the House of Commons.

maintopic: SPEER. TELEGRAM FROM HIS HONOUR THE SPEAKER AND DR. SPEER'S
speechtext: Adding insult to injury.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SPEER. TELEGRAM FROM HIS HONOUR THE SPEAKER AND DR. SPEER'S
speechtext:
The race track men of course had the money. My thought was not that money was used in the sense of bribery, but in keeping men there. We were berated by one speaker because we did not send letters. The words "foregone conclusion " referred to the fact that after the war was over this matter of racing would come back. I did not leave the impression on the Conference that I thought it a foregone conclusion that the Government would stand in with the race track people. I greatly regret that a false impression was left by the half dozen sentences which X uttered on this question. I shall be glad Sir, if you will make the substance of this telegram clear to the members of the House.
J. C. Speer.
I have only this to say, that I think it is in the highest degree unfortunate that such loose language should be indulged: in by persons holding responsible positions, and that the press should be so careless in the matter of making reports as to enable language, capable of the interpretation which could be placed upon the despatch of yesterday, to go broadcast throughout the country.

maintopic: SPEER. TELEGRAM FROM HIS HONOUR THE SPEAKER AND DR. SPEER'S
speechtext:
Does the House accept
this as an apology from Dr. Speer, and is the matter closed? I think his explanation makes it worse.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SPEER. TELEGRAM FROM HIS HONOUR THE SPEAKER AND DR. SPEER'S
speechtext: It is entirely a question for the House.

speechtext: I think the best policy would have been to have ignored the whole matter. This man now states "I said what I am reported to have said but I do not mean it." He must take us for a lot of children. I cannot regard his aetion as otherwise than extremely foolish.

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the other day I brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice the fact that two brothers named Labrie, who have been sentenced to twenty-five years in the penitentiary had been released on Habeas Corpus proceedings and then re-arrested. I noticed in last night's Montreal paper that Mr. Justice Duelos, who presided over the Habeas Corpus proceedings, has ordered the imprisonment of the Warden of the St. Vincent de Paul. Penitentiary for failure to produce the Labrie brothers in court.

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.
speechtext:
For contempt of court.
Mr, LEMIEUX:-and he makes certain comments on the action taken by the officers of the Crown. So that I may not be ruled out of order, Mr. Speaker, I should explain that this is a case of Habeas Corpus proceedings, where the liberty of the subject is involved. The remarks of Mr. Justice Duelos are as follows:
I am informed, that in disobeying the order of ithe court, the warden of the penitentiary ds acting under orders of some authority, and I will say without hesitation that it is high time that these authorities be shown that instead of hindering the process of justice they should do their utmost to facilitate it. I do not know who issued this order to disobey the order of the Superior Court, but whether it is the Minister of Justice of Canada or the Attorney General of this province, I say that they are giving a terrible example and one which can only do great harm to the respect and reputation tribunals are entitled to.
I know what the right hon. Minister of Justice will say in regard to the proceedings themselves-he has given his opinion based on the report of the Deputy Minister of Justice-but what is most serious in my judgment is that not only are the poor. Labrie brothers arrested, but that the warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary has been sentenced to one year's imprisonment.
I would like to know what my right, hon. friend has to say in the matter. Before long he may be arrested himself for all I know, and I would be very sorry if that should happen.

There is a conflict between two courts, one a court of undoubted criminal jurisdiction which has ordered the warden of the Kingston penitentiary

speechtext:
All right. It is absolutely immaterial. It is an order of the Superior Court; take it that wav. The other order is of the Court of King's Bench. The order of the Superior Court purports to issue under a statute which provides that its provisions shall not have application when men are held detained under conviction of a properly constituted criminal tribunal.
Now, before it is suggested that there is anything in the nature of contempt in the action of the warden or of any one who advised him, might I call attention to his position? He is between the two courts with their diametrically contradictory orders. How much more wicked is it for him to disobey the order of the Superior Court than it would be for him to disobey the order of the Court of King's Bench? He is advised that the court which has jurisdiction in the matter is the criminal court that sentenced these men, and he is advised that the court which purported to make this order of habeas corpus is without jurisdiction.

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.
speechtext:
I personally take my
full share of responsibility for that advice. But as the hon. gentleman is curious about it

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
subtopic: THE CASE OF THE LABRIE BROTHERS.
speechtext:
-I might quote what may be described as the advice of the Supreme Court of Canada on precisely the same subject. I am not going to argue the case, but I want to read this extract because it shows exactly what the position is. This is the opinion of Chief Justice Ritchie of the Supreme Court of Canada in rendering the judgment of that court in the case of re Sproule, which will be found in 12 Supreme Court Reports. After citing a number of authorities, be said:
The general rule is well established that a person imprisoned under the sentence of a court having general jurisdiction of the case is not to be discharged by habeas corpus, but should be left to his remedy by appeal, exceptions, or writ of error.
These authorities are, to my mind, conclusive that If the prisoner has any just cause of complaint against the proceedings in this case his remedy, if any exists, cannot be obtained through the instrumentality of a writ of habeas corpus, for I have no hesitation in saying that a judgment of conviction and sentence of the court of oyer and terminer and general gaol delivery of British Columbia-
I presume the hon. gentleman would not suggest that the judgment of a like court in the province of Quebec is not entitled to the same respect.
-on an indictment for murder, confirmed on error by the Supreme Court of British Columbia-
The case had been appealed and was confirmed, but the principle is' exactly tihe same.
-and standing unreversed by the Privy Council is conclusive as to the prisoner being a convicted felon.
That was a case of murder; this is a case of manslaughter.
Such a decision as this on which we are called to pass-
The decision with which we are concerned is precisely the same in principle as the decision there referred to, but the latter was rendered by a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada.
Such a decision as this on which we are called to pass raises a conflict of authority-
That is the source of any conflict of authority in this case.
-between the established Superior Courts of the country and individual judges of a most



extraordinary character; places the officer in whose custody the prisoner ie,-
And this is what I was endeavouring to point out.
-in this most anomalous and trying position, compelling him to elect to hold the prisoner under the judgment and sentence of a court of unquestionably competent criminal jurisdiction, confirmed by the unanimous decision of the full bench of the Supreme Court of the province having unrestricted jurisdiction in criminal eases, or to discharge him under the order of a single judge at chambers, it may be even of a single judge of the very court that unanimously affirmed his judgment and sentence, or a single judge of this court in direct opposition to, and defiance of, 6uch a conviction and sentence.	,
Now, the warden attended with the writ actually endorsed in the identical terms which the Supreme Court in the case I have been citing determined to he a proper and sufficient return. Unfortunately the summons being for half past ten. counsel got into the wrong room in the court house, and before the error was discovered the court had proceeded, with no return before it, to order the release of the prisoner. Fortunately, however, there was not an absolute order, as I am informed, for the imprisonment of the warden. That order, as I am told, 'was issued in the form of a rule nisi so that the warden wild have opportunity next Monday to show cause why he- should not be subject to the imprisonment referred to. I have thought it proper, and have been glad of the opportunity to make this statement because certainly St would be most regrettable if there should be any feeling on the part of any of the authorities concerned that there is any desire to do other than ensure a proper respect for the courts. We owe respect to, and I have the most profound respect for, the Superior Court of my provihce. I am prepared to go further and to say that, speaking of the individual judge, I have the most profound respect for him and entertain a very high opinion both of his abilities and of his character. But my respect extends to all the courts; it goes out just as wholly to the Court of King's Bench, the court charged with the administration of criminal justice, as it does to the Superior Court. Now, if all who- are interested will just possess their souls in patience, I undertake to say that pursuant to our very sincere desire-that is the desire, too, of the provincial authorities-we shall endeavour to find a method by which this question can be judicially and finally decided by the courts. In the meantime we cannot but feel-and1 it is a feeling common to the provincial authorities and to
[Mr. Doherty. J	1 j
ourselves-that it is our duty not to allow a judgment of the Court of King's Bench to be set aside in the way in which it has been and remain unexecuted without, at all events, having exhausted the means which the law affords for having the matter finally and properly determined.

The idea of that tax is that silk is to some extent a luxury. It is a very nice thing and we all like to see it worn in the becoming way it is worn by the ladies, but still it is a luxury, and we think that people who can afford to buy silk might well be asked to pay a tax on it. In a climate like ours silk of itself cannot be looked upon as a necessity. In hot weather cottons are cheaper, and in our cold weather silk is hardly the thing. Before we proceed further with this resolution I must remind the committee that a motion has been agreed to which provides for its consideration paragraph by paragraph and item by item. I certainly cannot interpret that to mean that hon. members of the committee can pick out special items at random and discuss them. Bourinot in his excellent work on parliamentary procedure states that when a Bill is taken clause by clause or paragraph by paragraph all amendments must be made in consecutive order, without unanimous congest the committee cannot amend the latter part of a Bill or resolution and then proceed to consider an amendment to the first paragraph. I can quite understand the position in which hon. members have been placed, and have no blame to offer nor any fault to find with any hon. member, but if the committee would agree with the Chairman I think we should take the resolution as it now stands with the proposed amendments, read it item by item, discuss each item as it is reached and reserve to hon. members the right to discuss any question concerning the principle of this form of taxation, or

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: My reference was not to antique furniture, but more particularly to those classes of furniture called veneers, which, as stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Parent), become quite expensive. It may be perfectly true that those articles of furniture are in a sense luxuries; probably they are. For example, a bedroom suite may run as high as $600, or $1,000, or $1,200. I do not think it is the intention of the minister to inflict any loss upon any manufacturers or any disability upon workmen engaged in those factories. In the city from whjch I come the' art of furniture making has been developed to a very high degree from the cheapest classes of furniture to the most expensive. It does not necessarily follow that manufacturers who are engaged in the business of making more expensive and artistic furniture, if you like, are in a position to stand any great financial loss. I am told that, as a result of the tax which has been imposed upon these more expensive lines of furniture, there has already been an enormous number of cancellations of goods which had been sold by the manufacturers. There is no doubt whatever that those men will have to suffer a very serious loss, because not only will they have those stocks left on their hands, but they have already prepared a considerable quantity of raw material in the way of expensive goods which cannot very well be adapted for any other kind of furniture than this particular kind. The suggestion has been mane to me-and it seems to me a fair one-is that these men, instead of being compelled to suffer this loss, should be given some opportunity of adapting themselves to the manufacture of other lines and should be enabled to sell what furniture they have already in stock and the material which must be made into that kind of furniture. This is a very serious matter to many manufacturers in this country, and perhaps the minister would give it some consideration.

The matter is specifically dealt with in the amended resolutions which were placed in Hansard but I do not think my hon. friend had the opportunity of looking at those proposals. Jewellery, as a rule, is sold by jewellers. But because it is not always sold by them, but is sometimes- sold by other people, it is necessary to retain these specific taxes which we have provided for and which the committee has been considering. It is proposed that they may obtain a license and not pay the specific taxes on these articles but pay ten per cent on the whole of their turn-over. The amended proposition is:
Cigar and cigarette holders and pipes in excess of $2.50 each; cigar and cigarette cases; ash trays and match-boxes of gold or silver, humidors, and smoking stands; hunting and bowie knives; gold and silver-handled pocket knives and pencils, and gold fountain pens; gold, silver and ivory toilet ware; articles of silver not otherwise provided for in this resolution adapted for household or office use ; silver or gold deposit ware; articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery, whether real or imitation, for personal use or for adornment of the person.

usually sold by the jeweller. Then we go on:

speechtext:
We are not
striking those words out at all, Mr. Chairman. I do not know that it really matters very much where this amendment is inserted. I think myself that it ought to form the subject matter of a separate section but it would be easier to insert it at the end of the section we are now considering, section (b).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Shall the last item of section (b) be carried before we consider this?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I notice that "articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery" are taxed at the rate of 20 per cent. I understand that it is the intention of the minister to tax the turn-over at 10 per cent.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: This item should be struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I understand the situation-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Shall this item carry, "articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery, whether real or imitation, for personal use or for adornment of the person"?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman; I have something to say on that item, if you will allow me. Notwithstanding the explanation of the minister, I do not like the idea of that section being adopted. But first I want to- draw his attention to what seems to me to be an anomaly. By a subsection he proposes to grant -a license, he has told us, to jewellery stores, or to departmental stores that have a jewellery branch; and any country departmental store that sells

jewellery may receive a license subject to a tax of 10 per cent. But if it should be contended that jewellery is not their chief business, it would seem to me that a question might arise whether they are entitled to a license. For example, I carry in my mind's eye at the moment several country stores whose chief business would not be jewellery, but they would have a show-case of jewellery on the counter and, if you like to so describe it, a small jewellery branch.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Cuff links.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I want to draw the minister's attention to that anomaly so- that he may provide for -a country store receiving a license t-o sell jewellery subject to the 10 per cent tax.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The regulations will cover that.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I do not know how regulations can run counter to what is in the Act. I am not very sure that it is right to- go into a jewellery store and pay 10 per cent on a certain article on which in another store you would have to pay 20 per cent. The minister tells us the reason is that the jeweller is paying a 10 per cent tax on all his stock. I admit there is some force in that circumstance, but I confess that I do not like the idea of this differentiation. A merchant who may not have a jewellery establishment may have some items of jewellery among his stock, for instance, cigar-holders and pipes. A man buys a pipe in a certain store and pays 20 per cent duty on his purchase, while in the next store he may be able to purchase a similar pipe and pay only .10 per cent duty. I do not know whether this can be overcome, but I am just drawing it to the minister's attention in the hope that he may be able to do away with this anomaly.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
By my previous remarks I do not wish it to be understood that I am desirous of making things hard for the ' jeweller. In fact I think that the proposal to bring the tax down to 10 per cent is a very good one. But I must say -that I do not believe that the proposition to have a flat rate of 10 per cent for jewellers is going to work out in practice. I agree with the former speaker (Mr. Loggie) in the illustrations he has given. Many tradesmen throughout the country handle jewellery as a side-line, for instance, stationers, fancy goods dealers and others. Now, if a jeweller in a large centre is t-o be charged only a 10 per cent rate on jewellery, and the trades-

man in the small town is to be charged 20 per cent on similar jewfellery that he handles as a side line, you are going to handicap the latter in his business, and I do not think that is the desire of the Government. I would suggest that the item be transferred to the 10 per cent section, and that no special license be necessary for jewellers.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I think the suggestion
made by the member for Brant (Mr. Harold) is absolutely fair. In addition to the classes of business mentioned by the member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) handling jewellery as a side line, I might mention gents' furnishing stores. It is an advantage to men going into such stores to be able to get cuff links and similar articles, but if a duty of 20 per cent is imposed on these articles when sold as a side line instead of 10 per cent when sold in jewellery stores, it will be a most unfair discrimination in favour of the latter. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Brant is a good one and should be adopted.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I also am strongly of opinion that this discrimination will create a great, deal of had feeling throughout the country. I think the suggestion of the member for Brant would meet the difficulty. It does seem entirely inconsistent that two men doing business side by side, the jeweller probably handling certain lines that are handled by his neighbour the 'tobacconist, should be treated in this way, one having 10 per cent and the other 20 per cent imposed on sales of similar articles. I realize the difficulty that confronts the minister, hut I am confident that this discrimination if permitted will create a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the whole country. It is something that cannot be supported as fair; it is an unjust discrimination which will be resented. The proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Harold) would be an easy way out of the difficulty and would possibly not materially affect the amount of taxes realized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
This is a nasty question; it is a difficult thing to get at. I suppose that really it depends upon which way you look at it. If we want to raise revenue, that is one thing; if, on the other hand, we want to be quite sure that the incidence of this 'taxation will be right in every single instance, why, we would never put on any taxes of this kind. Now, here is the great trouble in connection with luxury and jewellery taxes. The tax on jewellery is so easy to evade that so far no
very great amount has been raised in luxury taxes upon it. These taxes are not a new thing in this country; we are supposed even now to have luxury taxes on jewellery. I suppose not many hon. gentlemen know that there is such a thing, unless they were actually engaged in considering these'sections when they went through. But there is a luxury tax on jewellery at the present time.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: In Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: In Canada; I am not at all surprised that the hon. member knows nothing about it. There is a direct tax on jewellery to-day as a luxury. We have collected very little revenue through it-I think about $732,000. From trade sources I am told that there are approximately 2,500 jewellery shops in Canada and that they do ,a business on the average of $40,000 a year. That makes a pretty large turn-over, about $100,000,000.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Retail business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Yes. A tax of ten per cent on that turn-over is a fairly large item. I do not think that we will get the whole of 10 per cent on that amount, because the chances are that this business will fall off. But let us turn now for a moment to the case that has been suggested, the tobacconist on the one side and the jeweller on the other. The tobacconist today is subject merely to a few specific luxury taxes, but every single thing the jeweller handles is subject to a ten per cent tax. If we say, to the tobacconist: You are paying ,a specific luxury tax on things which are, after all, foreign to your business; would you rather pay ten per cent on the whole amount of your turn-over? You would not find one tobacconist who would want to do it. The sale of these things by the tobacconist constitutes only a small percentage of his business. If that is not so, I would gladly put the tobacconist in the same position as the jeweller and impose a tax of 10 per cent on his gross sales. And surely it is not any hardship on the dry goods merchant to be told that if he goes into a side line which may be looked upon as a luxury, he must pay taxes on the goods in which he so dekls, because another person engaged in that business has to pay ten per cent on his whole turn-over. The dealer who goes into the jewellery business as a side-line finds that the goods -are subject to a 20 per cent tax in respect of the particular items while the jeweller pays 10 per cent on his whole turn-over; but

many things which jewellers sell are sold by other people without the imposition of tax. I think that all things will pretty well even up with each other. The great underlying necessity, after all, is the necessity for revenue. It does seem to me that we can better get a' revenue in this way and that there will not be very much difficulty when other people understand that they can get exactly the sort of treatment the jewellers are getting if they themselves want it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I appreciate the efforts the minister is making to meet the situation and also the difficulties which have been suggested, particularly the difficulty which several hon. members have suggested of having a tax rate of 10 per cent on an article in one shop and 20 per cent on a similar article sold in another shop. But can we not avoid that by making a distinction between the different classes of jewellery? Suppose we retain the wording of this item:
Articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery, whether real or imitation, for personal use or adornment of the person.
Add the words "not otherwise provided for," put that item in the ten per cent list; then repeat the item in the 20 per cent list in the case of articles of jewellery of value greater than J}50. Then you have no question of discrimination between different stores; you have the same tax on a given article, no matter where it is sold, but you make a distinction between the moderately-priced article and the high-priced article which is unquestionably a luxury.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
(If the hon.
member would change his value say to $2 he would then cover pretty nearly all the articles of jewellery that are carried in dry goods stores,-collar buttons and all that kind of thing. Perhaps we could make it $5 and transfer it to the 10 per cent tax/ making the present item refer merely to jewellery selling at mofe than $5 per piece.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I do not know that my hon. friend has caught my point. I would make a distinction between expensive jewellery and inexpensive jewellery. Just what is the proper figure for inexpensive items may be a matter of debate. I suggested $50; make it less if you like, but make provision that the rate shall be the same no matter where the article is sold. Let there be no discrimination.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I do not propose to
attempt to sketch in detail what the min-

ister should do in connection with this matter, but I do say with great confidence that the minister must not tax an article at 20 per cent in one store and at 10 per cent in another. That goes to the very foundation of proper taxation. The tax must be equal; if it is upon goods, goods of the same value, wherever found, must pay the same tax. The minister speaks about the necessity for obtaining revenue. We are all with him in that but to commit a flagrant injustice in collecting revenue would in the long run defeat the very object that was had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Will the hon. member point out where the flagrant injustice is and who is affected by it? Is it on the jeweller, or is it on the other person who is selling cheap jewellery? We are suggesting that the other person will be willing to take the same terms that the jeweller takes; and if the injustice be on the jeweller, the matter of fact is that jewellers prefer this method because they know that, with their clerks handling the many different lines that are handled, it would be impossible to carry out the law in any other -way, because things can be so easily manipulated in that business. If there be any injustice to anybody, the way to clear it up is first to define the injustice and not to talk in generalities. Who is hurt-the jeweller or the other man?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The other man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Then the other man can have the same opportunity as the jeweller of taking out a license and paying 10 per cent on his turn-over. -

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Will the license not cost him money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: There is nothing in the license. He can take out a license and pay 10 per cent on his turn-over.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: But will that turn-over include other articles than jewellery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Yes. We are doing this with the jeweller, because he handles so many things which are really luxuries. He has to pay, for example, on things that may be sold by a hardware man, but he will pay the tax just the same. This tax includes the whole of his turn-over, on the theory that the articles sold are really luxuries. There is no tax on any article as1 such when sold by a jeweller; the tax is gone. The fact is that if you purchase something from a man who does not pay the whole 10 per cent on his turn-over, jmu pay a tax on that article,

but you can go to the jeweller and you will be charged no tax except what the jeweller chooses to put on, which may be a good deal more in order to cover the tax.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: How does that apply to large departmental stores which carry jewellery? Will they pay 10 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Any person engaged in the jewellery business and in the class of articles a jeweller ordinarily handles which may not be subject t-o any tax at all, will, if he chooses to take out a license, be given exactly the same treatment as. a jeweller.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The minister has not put
that proposition before the committee in these resolutions.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The present suggestion of the minister that it will be necessary for a departmental store in a country place carrying the same articles as a jeweller would carry in a city, to take out a license, is, to my mind, impracticable. If you attempted to carry out that suggestion, you would find that stores in country places would be discriminated against, because while they might carry jewellery, they certainly would not carry many of the articles that are supposed to be carried by jewellers in cities. What I understood was that, even in a Country place, any departmental store that had a jewellery department, would be entitled to get a license for whatever articles they kept that would come under this list. That is why I drew the attention of the minister to the word "chief," because this would not be the chief business of a departmental store in a small town. The minister's explanation now is that a departmental store in a small town can get a license provided that it carries the other class of goods usually carried by jewellers in large cities. That class of goods is not sold in departmental stores in small towns, and I should like the minister to consider the matter and strike out the word "chief." You could, not say that Eaton's jewellery branch was the chief business that firm was engaged in.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: What about Woolworth's five, ten and fiften cent stores?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That is another consideration altogether. Can departmental stores in small towns take out licenses to sell jewellery and everything else that they carry that is included in this list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
They can. There is no difficulty about that at all. That is the idea; but if they do that, they have to do it subject to regulations, and those regulations
will provide that whatever they sell-they do not have to put into stock all articles of the kind that a city jeweller handles- which would ordinarily be sold by a jeweller or form part of a jeweller's ordinary business, whether it was jewellery or otherwise, would have to be included in that department, and the 10 per cent would have to be paid on all that.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That would be all right.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: What the minister proposes may be an improvement on his first resolution, but I think he has still failed to give careful consideration to the suggestion I made. Why should there be any need of a license? Why should we have to have a turn-over tax in the case of a jeweller? Why should we have any question as to difference of rates as charged on any article of jewellery in one shop or another? Why should the minister not provide that on any article up to a value of $50, say, the tax shall be 10 per cent, and if the value is more than $50, the tax shall be 20 per cent? I see no difficulty in that and if there be a difficulty, nobody has suggested it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I would meet the suggestion made by my hon. friend, but to a much smaller extent in value than is suggested is too high. It kills the object of stores carrying cheap lines of jewellery, generally cheap cuff links, collar buttons and that sort of thing, just for the convenience of customers, not because they want to make anything out of the matter at all. I know I 'have bought things of that sort there myself. If you were to make the item read:
Articles commonly or commercially known as Jewellery, whether real or imitation, for personal use for adornment of the person, at a price not exceeding some nominal sum, perhaps $2, $3, $4 or $'5.
The case would.be met as regards that particular part of the trade.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: One cannot buy much except trash in a jewellery shop for $2.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The tax-of 20 per cent as
suggested is too high. It kills the object of the resolution: first, it kills the business of the man who is handling the goods, because he will find it difficult to sell goods which are subject to a 20 per cent tax and, second, revenue will not be obtained because the business will be killed. If the tax were lower, the hon. member's suggestion, would be better.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The difficulty that presents itself is. as regards discrimination, and another way of meeting that difficulty is worthy of consideration. There are in the schedule a few items on which a higher duty is imposed than that imposed upon jewellers. The list, which is enumerated, is not a very large one. Certain of those articles are ones which a jeweller invariably carries, for instance, fountain pens, pencils, humidors', etc. which are really foreign to his business although he has a perfect right to carry them. Why cannot a tax of 10 per cent be imposed upon the jeweller except on items otherwise specified in the schedule which bear a higher rate and which he may carry in stock? A jeweller would have no difficulty in keeping track of sales made of humidors, fountain pens, pencils, etc. In that way the difficulty would be got over. No matter how much we may apologize for or try to explain the difficulty Parliament is supposed to surmount difficulties, and you cannot call it a just or sound principle to impose a different rate of taxation on two stores side by side selling the same articles. If it is not possible for the minister to meet this difficulty now, I would suggest that the item be postponed for further consideration, for trouble is bound to arise from any such discrimination as is here proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I beg to add after the word "person" in this item the words "in excess of five dollars," and also to add to sub-paragraph (a) the item:
Articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery whether real or imitation, for personal use or for the adornment of the person not exceeding $5 in value.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I entirely approve of this step but I think the figure is too low. You cannot buy much for $5 in a jewellery shop. If my hon. friend wants to make any concession to the average middle-class person, the figure should be more than $5. However, if that is his determination, we Cannot help it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I should just like to say, in view of the remarks I have made, that I am entirely satisfied with the resolutions as they now stand, which seem to me to meet the situation very well.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend sub-paragraph (b) by adding thereto the following:
Any person, firm or corporation, including the jewellery branch of a departmental store whose chief business is the selling of jewellery by retail, shall obtain a special license to sell jewel-

lery and other articles specified in this resolution, in which case the tax payable shall be 10 per centum on the value of the total sales of such establishment or branch, under regulations to be made by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
(c) A tax of fifty per cent on :-
Articles of gold not otherwise provided for in this resolution adapted for household or office use.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: What are these articles of gold not otherwise provided for? A fifty per cent tax is almost prohibitive, and it would be interesting to know just what this item covers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Solid gold plate, for instance, gold dining services, solid gold boxes.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Do you expect to get much revenue from that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: None I think, but the tax may prevent some gold being used in that way.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If you reduced the tax to 10 or 15 per cent you would have a chance of getting some revenue, but with the 50 per cent tax you will get none at all from this source.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: It is to prevent gold being used for these purposes, not to raise revenue.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Would not this be the proper place to provide that wedding rings shall be excepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: There is no reason in the world why that should not go in, and I have pleasure in moving to add the words "except wedding rings."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Engagement rings too?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: 1 am afraid I cannot go as far as that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Shall sub-paragraph (c) carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
With the amendment which I have suggested, "not including gold pen nibs."

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I must point out to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) that by imposing a tax of 50 per cent on all articles of gold " not otherwise provided for" he is taxing very heavily gold medals that are given by colleges, schools and other institutions by way of reward to pupils. I do not think it is the intention of the minister to tax these articles, and I fancy it must have escaped his attention. I would therefore ask him to reconsider the item, and possibly amend it so as to except from its operation these gold medals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: In view of the general tax on jewellers of ten per cent of the turnover, as suggested, I think my hon. friend will see that the medals, which are always made by jewellers, will not be affected at all.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

II should like to make a suggestion the adoption of which would greatly simplify this provision. In the business in which I am directly interested, many boats and motor boats are required, and if the minister allows this resolution to pass as it stands, be is going to impose a great hardship upon a number of men who live in out-of-the-way places,

not only manufacturers but men who purchase these boats. 'Perhaps the minister is aware that in the different fishing settlements', not only on the Nova Scotia coast but on the New Brunswick coast, the Gasp6 coast and also the Pacific coast, there are men who are known as boat-builders. Such a man may get an order for one boat, a dory of 20 feet in length, or a small boat of the same length, but of a different pattern, or a motor boat of small size intended for fishing purposes, or a large boat intended for off-shore fishing. These boat-builders are situated sometimes on islands and other out-of-the-way places along the different coasts. They are not boat-builders in the ordinary sense of the term; they are not business men, and they keep no accounts. A man may come to one of them and ask him to build a dory or half a dozen dories, and when the contract is completed, the man comes and -pays the

amount and no acoount is kept ol the transaction. The minister could simplify the matter very much if he would amend the clause to read:

If they are responsible or reliable citizens, they are not going to sell pleasure boats and call them commercial boats. So the minister's argument falls to the ground. There is a distinct difference between commercial and pleasure boats. No man can got a pleasure boat built for him and call it a commercial

boat, because there is a distinction between the two which the builder and the owner cannot get over. Therefore, instead of running around getting some man to certify that the boat which he built for John 9 p.m. Jones was a commercial boat or a pleasure boat, I think it would be more businesslike if the minister adopted some such simple suggestion as I have made which covers the ground absolutely and would avoid all trouble.

a large class of boats that I think, some hon. members are losing sight of altogether. On the inland waters of this country, I believe, there are half a dozen canoes to every motor boat or any other type of boat. The manufacturers of these canoes make identically the same canoe for commercial and pleasure purposes, and ship them out in carload lots to different parts of the country. Perhaps half are purchased for commercial purposes and the other half for pleasure. The manufacturer pays the tax without any idea whether the canoes he ships are going to be used for pleasure or commercial purposes. In the district where I live these canoes are bought by prospectors for running the rivers and lakes, and by the Indians for trapping purposes. As many of them are used in that way as for pleasure, and the boat is identically the same.

I do not know why you should toe so considerate about chewing gum. I think gum chewing is one of the most vulgar habits that exists in this country. Recently I read an article, written by a gentleman who had resided for several years in Brazil, describing how the gum was collected -and treated, and he added, "If the people only knew what enters into chewing gum, they would not touch it with a ten-foot pole." I have heard that when the "Sammies" were crossing the Atlantic "to win the war" a young lady having asked General Pershing what comforts she should collect for the Sammies, he replied: "For Heaven's sake suppress gum for the soldiers, because they will see the nice French girls, and those girls will probably copy the habit of chewing gum, and then they will change the brightest smile in the world into the most awful grimace." subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
If I understand the
amendment well, there is a reduction from 30 (to 20 per cent on patent medicines. I appreciate the reduction, but I contend, Mr. Chairman, that that tax should be removed altogether. During the Budget debate I quoted the comments of the Ottawa Journal on this matter. I may say that when the minister announced that he was going to reduce the tax from 30 to 20 per cent 'the Journal went on and said that in its opinion the tax was still too high and gave very good reasons for it. It contended that it is the sick who are to be taxed, and especially the poorer people who are sick. It further said that patent medicines are often the poor man's substitute for profes-ional medical attention. I think the point made by that paper is very well taken. I will state further that this tax is imposed on the poor people when they are less able to pay it, because when they are sick their earnings are either impaired or they do not receive any at all by reason of the fact that they cannot work. The minister is taking off taxes from food. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that medicine is properly the food of the sick people and it should not be taxed at all. The alcohol that is contained in patent medicines is not a beverage, it is merely a preservative. If these medicines are found on analysis to contain more alcohol than is necessary to preserve their contents they are discarded, or if they do not contain sufficient medicinal elements they are discarded. So it is quite plain that a patent medicine cannot he described as a beverage; it is merely a food for sick people. I would ask the minister-when he comes in-to remove that tax altogether. There is no doubt the Government will lose a little revenue but that loss will accrue to the advantage of the hospitals and sick people and, I think, will not be out of place.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
As I understand the amendment, it makes this change in the resolution as originally introduced, that the manufacturer of a medicinal preparation is obliged to pay the increased tax of $2 per proof gallon upon the alcohol that enters into the manufactured product. That means a duty of $3.30 a gallon for absolute alcohol. The tax of 30 per cent
on patent medicine, or the reduced rate of 20 per cent, is a customs tax which will operate as a countervailing tax to protect the domestic manufacturer against imported remedies manufactured in the United States or any other country and not subject to the additional tax upon alcohol. The same would apply to the $2 per gallon flat tax which is afterwards provided for in the resolution, and which will apply as a customs tax upon imported medicinal preparations that do not come under the classification of patent or proprietary medicines, and upon perfumes and toilet preparations containing alcohol. In both cases the tax applies only to those preparations containing alcohol.
The position under the proposed amendment is that there is no tax upon medicinal preparations containing alcohol manufactured in Canada, aside from the tax of $2 per proof gallon, which amounts to $3.30 a gallon upon the alcohol which enters into the manufacture. I might say that the tax of $2 per proof gallon, or $3.30 a gallon upon the alcohol which enters into the product, is a' very severe charge in itself, and it is in order to protect the domestic manufacturer that the tax upon patent medicines and the flat tax of $2 per gallon is put on as a customs tax or countervailing charge. In no case is there a tax upon a proprietary or patent medicine or medicinal preparation of any kind that does not contain alcohol.
In addition there is a tax exemption on alcohol where it enters into the manufacture of preparations from which it cannot be recovered. Under our Inland Revenue law to-day there is power by Order in Council-which has been exercised for years-to reduce the tax of $2.40 per proof gallon to 15 cents. Take the alcohol, for instance, used in the manufacture of Sal-varsan. A large amount o.f alcohol is required for crystallization, in the manufacture of that remedy, and the alcohol so used comes in under a tax of 15 cents. There is quite a range of other preparations, such as chloroform, etc., where the alcohol used is lost in the process o.f manufacture. Under this amendment, as I understand it, where alcohol is used in the manufacture of these preparations-and, as I say, there are quite a number of them-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Would ether be included in that?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Yes. Where the alcohol is used and lost it is not subject
to the tax. The necessity for that exemption

will be present to the minds of the committee when we consider that under the law as it has existed for years provision has been made in order that the Canadian manufacturer might be in a position to compete with the foreign manufacturers of these products. The same thing applies to perfume. Alcohol, which costs the manufacturers of almost all other products except thiose I have mentioned an inland revenue tax of $2.40, is passed for these manufacturers at a tax of 75 cents. Alcohol used in the manufacture of soap-and quite a lot is used-now comes in at 15 cents instead of $2.40.
Therefore the tax now imposed upon the manufacturer of medicinal preparations will be limited to the tax of $2 per proof gallon on alcohol. In the past the manufacturer of medicinal preparations has been forced to pay the same tax as if the alcohol were used for beverage purposes. The underlying reason is that it would be a comparatively easy matter to regulate the alcohol which enters into the manufacture of medicinal preparations where those preparations are manufactured by a pharmaceutical manufacturer, but the difficulty would be to control alcohol, suitable for beverage purposes, where it goes out into the hands of 3,300 retail druggists; and it would be manifestly unfair that those druggists should be obliged to pay the full alcohol tax-which at present is $3.95 per gallon-and in addition $3.30, or a total tax on alcohol after this .amendment is passed of $7.25-the pharmaceutical manufacturer should be relieved from the additional $3.30 tax. It has been because of the difficulty of controlling alcohol where it passes into the hands of so many retail druggists that it has been thought wise that the manufacturer of pharmaceutical preparations should be placed in precisely the same 'position as the retail druggist. Under this amendment it seems to me that the manufacturer of pharmaceutical preparations, the dealer in them, and the people who use them, are protected as far as possible if the additional tax of $2 is to go upon ethyl alcohol.

speechtext:
I do not
see why the poor man who requires a drug that needs alcohol to dissolve it should pay a tax because he has to take that drug to get well. Alcohol is sometimes required in OTder that a drug may be made soluble and capable of being administered to the human system. In that case the alcohol is not a beverage; it is simply a vehicle for the conveyance of certain drugs to the alimentary tract in such a manner that they can be assimilated and, may possibly assist in curing a disease. 1 do not see why proprietary medicines containing alcohol should be taxed any more than those which do not. I make no request concerning patent medicines, perfume, or anything of that kind, but I; do ask the minister to be generous and to cut out this provision with regard to proprietary medicines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
It is not a matter of what one would like to do; it is a matter of the desirability of having different rates of taxation upon alcohol in different forms. If the hon. member could show us how to overcome the difficulty I should be glad to consider the matter. But there are a large number of places where these

medicines are put up, and it would be impossible to police them. We cannot very-well increase the rate on alcoholic beverages without increasing the rate on medicines in' which alcohol is used.
Mr. BElLAND:	I share the view of my
hon. friendi from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) that patent medicines should not be too heavily taxed. They are bought largely by people who live in the country, particularly those who live a long distance from a physician; in many such cases they serve a goodi purpose. It would be a hardship to impose a heavy tax upon a patent medicine on the ground that it contains alcohol.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I suppose my
hon. friend 'knows of that wonderful beverage known as "Tanlac," which is so widely advertised and which is supposed to make such a first-rate cock-tail, and of "IBeef, Iron and Wine," which is often taken ad lib. There are many others of the kind.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I am not familiar with
the composition of "Tanlac," but none of these drugs can be sold unless their sale is authorized by the board constituted under a statute passed by this House at the last session.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I certainly
agree that there is no logical reason why the alcohol that enters into the manufacture of a medicinal preparation should be subject to a tax any more than any other of the medicinal ingredients should. We have provided that in the case of patent medicines a board composed of eminent .members of the medical profession shall pass upon the sufficiency of the medication. It has been found necessary to a'dd to the cost of medicines every increase that occurs in the tax upon alcohol for beverage purposes. There is a real objection to this, for the reason that the tax on patent and [DOT]proprietary medicines, and even on medicines that are dispensed on a doctor's prescription, comes out of people who actually require the medicine; and it seems to me that, as a matter of cold reasoning and logic, it would be far more reasonable to tax a man's oatmeal when he is in health and working and earning money than to tax his medicine when he is laid aside and his earning power has gone. The difficulty has always been to work the matter out in such a way as would permit the Government to control the alcohol. I can see quite plainly where it would be possible to control the alcohol that is used by a large pharmaceutical manufacturer in such a way as to protect the Government against
the improper use of alcohol for beverage purposes. But the difficulty that arises is in treating equitably all those engaged in dispensing medicinal preparations. It would be absolutely impossible to control the handling of alcohol in the hands of 3,300 retail druggists. The reason it would be easy to control a manufacturer is that every manufacturer -to-day manufactures in bond for export, because on his export trade he gets a rebate on the alcohol that enters into his product. The fact that he is so equipped, and that his premises are so laid out that he can manufacture under inland revenue supervision and that his products can be sent aside in bonded warehouses, enables the Government to keep an actual control upon the whole process of manufacture, and they are able to determine to a certainty the quantity of alcohol that enters into the manufacture of any particular product. But it is impossible to do that with the retail trade, and the difficulty that would arise in making any further concession here would be that you would be discriminating in favour of the large manufacturer as against the smaller manufacturer and the retail druggist who are not equipped to take advantage of any provision that might be made to relieve them of the alcohol tax.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I speak subject to correction because I have not heard the resolution very well; but one matter that was brought to my attention by a committee of the University of Manitoba was the use of ethyl alcohol in hospitals for bathing fever patients to prevent bed-sores, and for rubbing and such like. Is it possible to allow that to come in free of this $2 tax? I can, of course, see the difficulty of controlling the matter, but I should like to have the point considered by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I do not know that that could be covered in the present Bill. If anything were to be done in that direction-and I quite sympathize with the object the hon. member has in view-it seems to me it ought to be done by way of remission under the Audit Act, when it was shown that the spirit had been employed for the purposes indicated-direct hospital use.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
How will 'these changes work out? Perhaps I can be most clear by giving a specific instance. Let us suppose that a manufacturer has invoiced, say on 3rd June, a certain parcel of patent medicine and has charged 30 per cent on this parcel. A change is being made. Suppos-

ing the customer has paid on the basis of 30 per cent. Will the customer have a. right to ask the manufacturer or wholesaler to return to him 10 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

In the vast majority of cases, you can never tell whom the refund is going to, and, further, in the larger number of transactions, the amount, as a matter of fact, is not at, all serious.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Supposing a customer has declined to pay the 30 per cent. Would the manufacturer be complying with the law if he were satisfied to take 20 per cent now on the face of his invoice?

speechtext: Before the matter that I have raised is disposed of, may I ask the minister whether a statute now exists that allows of a refund in such a case as I have mentioned?

On some preparations the difference would run as much as 50 per cent. '

nection, in most proprietary medicines the percentage of alcohol is not high-there will be very little difference in the cost, for the reason, that undoubtedly a considerable proportion of the increased tax will be absorbed by the manufacturers.

speechtext: As a medical man, may I say a word in support of the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) and urge upon the minister the necessity of working out that section of the Act so that hospitals shall get a rebate on alcohol which they necessarily use in their duties towards patients? subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I wish to voice my very
strong objection to this tax of 30 cents a gallon on beer. As I had occasion to remark when speaking on the Budget, it seems outrageous that we should tax the beverage of the workingman 30 cents per gallon. I notice that there is bracketed with ale and beer, wines of all kinds, that is to say, all will be taxed 30 cents per gallon. As I have already said, previous to this tax the cost of beer to the workingman was about 30 cents per gallon. With this tax of 30 cents per gallon added, the price of his beer will be raised from 5 to 10 cents a glass. In other words, you are increasing the cost of the beverage of the poor man 100 per cent. It is not the same in the case of wines, which usually retail at about $3, $4 or $5 a gallon. A tax of 30 cents a gallon on wine is only a very small fraction of the cost, and wine is mostly partaken of by other than the poorer class. Why the poor man should have his beverage increased by 100 per cent, while the rich man's beverage should be increased only 10 or 12 per cent, passes my understanding. I have no doubt the minister will be able to give the House some explanation.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) has said. I think that, instead of imposing a flat rate of 30 cents per gallon, the minister should have taxed these beverages on a percentage basis. To tax beer and wine at the same flat rate seems to me to be wrong. The tax should be on a percentage basis.

I notice that in all the other cases where delegations called upon him and made him see that he was quite wrong in many of his conclusions, relief was obtained, but there was nobody to look after the interests of the workingman, and he now finds his beer advanced in price by 100 per cent.

5. That every person selling or dealing in the articles upon which taxes are imposed as prescribed by the foregoing resolutions may be required by the minister to take out an annual license therefor, for which license a fee not exceeding $2 shall be paid.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
In the debate that
took place on the Budget it was stated that this license might be revoked or cancelled if it were found that the dealer had violated any of the provisions of the Taxation Act in any respect whatever. I am not sure whether that statement is contained in the minister's speech, but I heard it from some one, and it appears' to me that this question might arise. If this power were used in any arbitrary way a merchant employing perhaps four or five hundred clerks might suddenly find himself held up on his license and entirely precluded from doing business by the fact that some one unknown to himself had made an error in not collecting a certain tax imposed among these hundreds of items embraced in these various resolutions. It seems to me that that is a question that should receive very careful consideration, and no arbitrary power should be exercised in any way in this respect. It is all right to require a license of $2, and between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand merchants will have to pay the fee. The resolution says that those who come uner this provision "may be required" to take out an annual license; I presume the minister means "shall be required." I cannot see why the word "may" is used; I suppose we can take it for granted that the minister will exact $2 from them. I submit to the minister that it would be rather a high-handed piece of

business to hold the merchant absolutely responsible all the time for all the transactions that are made by his entire staff throughout his shop or warehouse. It is a very large order in many cases, and men with the hest intentions will make mistakes and be subject to lapses of memory. I have known, in. the operation of the drug tax, cases where individuals have been fined $50 for the mistakes of clerks. These mistakes were not intentional, but the penalty was exacted in many cases, and I know of a few such cases in my own riding. Perhaps a small penalty might be provided. But to hold it over the head of the merchant or other vendor that if he does not live up to all the requirements of his license with regard to the hundreds of taxes we are enacting, then his license may be cancelled, is a very dangerous matter. It does not say in this particular section that this will be done, but I have heard that argument put forth; and it seems to me that the minister should so provide that a man will not be put out of business because he has been the innocent victim of a mistake or a piece of forgetfulness on the part of some of his staff. He cannot possibly exercise supervision over all their actions, and it would certainly be unjustifiable to put a man out of business if he did not comply with all the details of the Act.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
This paragraph reads:
" Every person selling or dealing in the articles upon which taxes are imposed as prescribed." That means every clerk in the employ of a store. The clerk would be the " person selling," and I do not think that it is the intention of the department that he should be required to obtain a license. " Proprietor " might be
better.

store is not " selling " in the sense intended in this paragraph. These people go around with packs on their backs and are neither merchants nor corporations; yet they sell and deal. We want to cover every one selling or dealing in these articles on his own account.

is the intention of the department, but it is not clearly expressed.

please answer my question? Is it intend-el that the license shall be revoked or cancelled, or even suspended for a time, in case it is not fully complied with?

the hon. member that we have no intention to try to enforce this Act vexatiously. We must, however, have some way of properly enforcing it. that requires firm and quick handling. But there is no thought of using that power harshly. It would be absolutely wrong to lo so, and more than that, it would be extremely foolish, for thereby the whole object of the Act would be defeated. On the other hand, it seems to me that the power shoull rest in the minister to see that firms do take reasonable precautions to ensure that the public revenue is protected.

I think we made that pretty clear. What is being settled now is only to keep ourselves in form. Nothing we have done is going to change the liability of merchants, or anybody else, to pay taxes. Everything stands as it is until the enabling Bill is brought down.
(a) That a tax of one per cent In addition to the present duties of excise and customs be imposed, levied and collected on sales by manufacturers, wholesalers, or on importations; that the purchaser shall be furnished with a written invoice of any sale, which invoice shall state separately the amount of such tax, when

not included in the purchase price; that such tax must not be included in the manufacturer's or wholesaler's costs on which profit is calculated ; and the tax shall be paid by the purchaser to the wholesaler or manufacturer at the time of such sale, and by the wholesaler or manufacturer to His Majesty in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed, and such wholesaler or manufacturer shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding $500, if such payments are not made, and in addition shall be liable to a penalty equal to double the amount of the excise duties unpaid.
A good many references have been made to this turn-over tax having particular regard to lines of business in which some manufacturers and producers sell direct in some instances, and in others where they sell to wholesalers. A good many complaints have been made, particularly from the West in connection with the lumber business where one firm, perhaps two firms, that are manufacturing lumber, sell direct to the public-having sub-stations at different towns apart from their headquarters-and do not sell to wholesalers, while in the great majority of cases the sale is to the wholesalers. The wholesalers object, as also do the smaller manufacturers to this tax entirely because they say it is placing the man who sells direct to the public and not to the wholesaler in a position of advantage to the extent of 1 per cent. I propose an amendment in connection with this so as to provide that when manufacturers sell direct to the consumers, the manufacturer in that case shall pay 2 per cent instead of the 1 per cent; and that whenever the importation is direct for the purposes of consumption there again the tax shall be 2 per cent, making both arrangements even.
The amendment therefore reads:
In addition to the present duty of excise and customs a tax of one per cent shall be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by manufacturers wholesalers, or jobbers and on the duty paid value of importations; that in respect of sales by manufacturers to retailers or consumers, or on importations by retailers or consumers the tax payable shall be two per cent, that the purchaser shall be furnished with a written invoice of any sale, which invoice shall state separately the amount of such tax to at least the extent of one per cent; that such tax must not be included in the manufacturer's or wholesaler's costs on which profit is calculated; and the tax shall be paid by the purchaser to the wholesaler or manufacturer at the time of such sale, and by the wholesaler or manufacturer to His Majesty in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed, and such wholesaler or manufacter shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding $500, if such payments are not made, and in addition shall be liable to a penalty equal to double the amount of the excise duties unpaid.

speechtext:
This is a serious tax on the firm that sells direct to the retail trade, and I happen to be connected with such a firm. We have to charge our customers in the retail trade 2 per cent on all the goods we sell them. It strikes me that great confusion will be caused, because the wholesaler charges only 1 per cent on his sales. Now, notwithstanding the fact that the wholesaler pays 1 per cent on what the manufacturer sells to him and then charges the retailer 1 per cent, I can see that he is placed in the same position indirectly as the manufacturer who sells direct to the retail trade. But what about the customer who gets an invoice from my concern, for instance, and finds that he is charged 2 per cent, while from the wholesale merchant he gets an invoice charging him only 1 per cent, and the price probably is the same? I fear it is going to create a great deal of dissatisfaction in the retail trade. This is a pretty heavy tax. I can easily understand that the Minister of Finance is after money, and we should all realize that we must pay. But this tax is going to raise a lot of money. The concern I am connected with does a business of $3,000,000 with the retail trade; a 2 per cent tax on that turnover is $60,000 a year; and besides that we are paying a tax of 1 per cent upon all the raw materials we buy, which taxes must be absorbed in the cost of the goods. As I said before, the Minister of Finance is 229i
after money, and I think he will get it, but I am afraid there is going to be a conflict between the *wholesaler and the manufacturer selling to the retail trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: We aTe dealing only with the concrete case of sales by manufacturers, wholesalers and jobbers, and importations. Whether a man is selling or not depends upon the question of fact, not upon the question of his description. If the manufacturers' agents are selling on a salary undoubtedly the sale is the manufacturer's. If they are agents selling on commission undoubtedly the 6ale again is the manufacturer's. Selling on commission the property never is the agent's, the risk is never his. He may look after the invoicing of goods, and very often does, but as a matter fact he is merely the means through which the manufacturer is selling. If we look at it in any other way we will be regarding i't as a double tax on the manufacturer and fixing another point at which the tax would be levied. We are not doing that. There are merely the two taxes. The position therefore is that if the Canadian manufacturer is working through an agent he pays, of course, his 1 per cent; if, on the other hand, the agent is working for an English manufacturer, that agent is in fact acting as importer either in his own capacity or on behalf of the manufacturer, and in that case he would pay 1 per cent. And, again, it would depend entirely upon the sale, because the tax is 1 per cent, but if he made it directly to the retailer or for consumption directly it would become 2 per cent whether imported or whether of local manufacture.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Will the minister explain the case of the 2 per cent?

speechtext: That will be exactly the same as the other case. If he were to sell direct to a retailer, leaving out the usual channels of business, he would then pay the 2 per cent. In other words, we get two turn-overs on the business.

speechtext:
The minister will understand the difficulty of the manufacturer who sells to the retail trade when he charges his customer two per cent. The wholesaler pays the manufacturer one per cent and he [Mr. Cocksh.utt.3
is permitted to absorb that one per cent in his cost,-to get it back from his customer in an indirect way to that the customer does not know he is paying it.
