speechtext:
In that case the retail
trade might also pass on the two per cent. A great many of them handle their goods at a very small margin and are finding considerable difficulty in absorbing that one per cent, whereas if they could hand down the two per cent the difficulty would be solved. But ll rose particularly to bring to the atten-tiofn of the minister an industry which should be specially dealt with in these resolutions,-the binder twine industry. Binder twine and the raw materials entering into its manufacture are on the free list. Under the present resolutions the binder twine industry will be discriminated against to the extent of nearly one per cent, and as one large institution that I know of has never paid a dividend equal to one per cent, it practically -means putting them out of business. If this two per cent clause is passed the American manufacturer will have to pay two per cent. If he sells through a jobber in Canada the jobber will pay one per cent and the American manufacturer will pay one per cent. If he sells direct to the retailer, two per cent will have to be charged at the time of importation. The Canadian manufacturer is in the same position in that respect,-he also will have to pay the two per cent tax, or it will be divided between himself and the jobber. But the Canadian manufacturer has to pay tax on his raw materials, which represent five-sixths of his cost. speechtext: The question is not so much where the goods were invoiced to as what was actually done. That which went into the wholesale establishment would be liable to the two per cent when it was sold to the public. subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The trend of modern business provides for a policy by which the manufacturer markets his goods, and everything that has occurred during the past ten years in the way of increasing economy in the management of business has taught both manufacturer and retailer that as many middlemen as possible should be eliminated. I appreciate the fact that in some instances the jobber or the wholesaler may be disriminated against where he has to pay on the invoice from the manufacturer a sales tax of one per cent and then pass on another one per cent to the retailer. But as the amendment now stands, I submit, the manufacturer is discriminated against. The manufacturer doing business to-day will sell to a jobber upon a basis that will enable the jobber to sell goods at the same price that the manufacturer does, provided the manufacturer also goes out and markets his goods direct. It is good business to do that; in fact, any other policy is practically impossible. If the manufacturer follows the policy of both marketing direct to the retailer and selling to the jobber he can afford to sell to the jobber cheaper than he can sell to the retailer because in connection with that branch of his business he is not obliged to keep a selling force. As a rule the jobber goes to the manufacturer's establishment and buys what he wants and his salesmen sell the goods to the retailer. In the large majority of cases the manufacturer keeps his own selling force so that his goods are sold at the same price by his travellers as they are sold at by the representatives of the wholesaler or the jobber. Now, what occurs? A retailer buys a line of goods from the salesman or from the sales force of the manufacturer, and at the same time he buys, or can buy, the same goods from the sales force of the jobber. He gets the invoices, and upon the invoice from the manufacturer he is charged a
sales tax of 2 per cent and upon the invoice from the jobber he is charged a sales tax of 1 per cent. That discriminates at once against the manufacturer and tends to create a condition where the manufacturer would reap an indirect advantage by marketing his goods indirectly through a jobber. There is this additional view, that after all the matter of values in buying is largely a matter of judgment, a mental condition on the part of the buyer. In the purchase of a very large range of commodities it is absolutely impossible for the buyer to form any absolute judgment, because the value depends so often upon things which are concealed and which it is impossible for him to determine, so that the matter is largely a mental condition. Suppose, acting on his judgment, he buys from a jobber a line of goods to sell at a certain price, and then he goes direct to the manufacturer and, again acting on his judgment, buys a competitive line of goods to sell at the same price. On the goods he buys from the manufacturer he has to pay 2 per cent of a sales tax as against 1 per cent of a sales tax he has to' pay on the goods he buys from the jobber. That is a condition that operates directly against a manufacturer who markets his goods directly.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: It operates against the public also.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Where a
jobber buys from a manufacturer, the manufacturer, under the provisions of the resolution, is bound to put upon the invoice as a separate entry a sales tax of 1 per cent. He pays that 1 per cent and he is permitted to absorb that 1 per cent into his cost. Upon that 1 per cent he is permitted to take a profit. But the 2 per cent, which the manufacturer is obliged to levy upon his direct sales from his factory to the retailer, he is not permitted to absorb at all, nor is he permitted to take any part of it into his cost. What I submit is this, that the average manufacturer would infinitely prefer to pay 1 per cent and absorb it himself rather than show upon his invoice double the amount that would be shown upon the invoice of the jobber or wholesaler. There may be certain lines where it might be found that 1 per cent was too large. There are a large number of lines in which jobbers do not intervene at all to-day and there are a large number of other lines where jobbers intervene to a very limited extent; but in my opinion, in every case where a line is marketed by the manufacturer him-

self directly and also marketed through a jobber, the manufacturer would infinitely prefer to pay and absorb one pet cent to being placed at the disadvantage at which he will be placed if he is obliged to put 2 per cent on his invoice when he sells directly to the retailer.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
In my judgment, the position taken :by the minister as regards this phase of the situation is absolutely correct. It is only reasonable to expect that the manufacturer and the wholesaler should be placed on absolutely the same level. We know 'from the wording of this resolution that the manufacturer will charge the wholesaler 1 per cent on his sales to the wholesaler, and consequently the wholesaler will add that to the cost of his merchandise and charge 1 per cent to the retailer, and these together, or 2 per cent, will be passed on to the Government. Why, then, should the manufacturer escape the 2 per cent that is paid in that transaction through the other avenue? It is absolutely fair, it is only simple justice, that that condition should operate and that the minister should pursue that' course. It obviates another difficulty. We know that many manufacturers sell direct to large retail stores and do not sell to small retailers at all. If the idea advocated by the 'hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Stewart) were listened to, these large departmental stores would be favoured to the extent of 1 per cent as against the small retailers. That would be absolutely unfair. I trust the minister will not consider that argument at all.
There is another feature in connection with the matter of the retailer buying directly from the manufacturer. On the admissions of the hon. member for Haldimand and the hon. member for Lanark the retailer gets no advantage in buying direct from the manufacturer, because the manufacturer will sell to the wholesaler at a lower price than he will sell to the retailer. Consequently, there is no advantage on the score of buying direct from the manufacturer excepting as regards the matter of delivery, and that is the point that influences the retailer in every instance in buying direct from the manufacturer. Therefore, in my judgment, it is an open question whether it is "more (economical for a retailer, small or large, to buy directly from a manufacturer or through the wholesale trade. As a matter of fact, from the admission made by my two hon. friends, who know ,what they are talking about, there is, from an economical point
IMr. J. A. Stewart.]
of view, no advantage to the retailer in
(buying direct from the manufacturer at the present time, because he knows that the manufacturer will not sell to the retailer as low as he will sell to the wholesaler; he will sell to the wholesaler at such a price that the wholesaler can, in turn, sell to the retailer at the same price as the manufacturer sells at direct to the retailer.
There is something in the argument put forward by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harold) as regards binder twine. That is a feature which, I am sure, will appeal to the minister, namely, that in the matter of raw material there is a discrimination against the home manufacturer, and consequently there would be a discrimination against the farming industry of this country. I am sure it is not the intention nor desire of this committee to penalize the farming industry of this country to any extent. We want to encourage farming in this country as much as we can. As regards the margin of taxation being absorbed in the cost of the manufactured goods, that is only a trifling amount, and the manufacturer passes it on in any event to the wholesaler or retailer so that there is no room for grumbling.
Another element to be considered is that of the agent, or salesman, or traveller- these three elements in distribution are one and the same thing. An agent may represent a European concern; but if he sells to the trade in this country, the importations come direct to the importer and not as a rule to the agent. When a salesman goes out direct to represent a manufacturer in this country selling domestic goods, he is on the same level exactly as a traveller representing a wholesale concern.
The hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said that there was a good deal of kicking about some of the features that are embodied in this particular section. If the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) will permit me, I will quote Scripture, and I am sure he will corroborate me in that quotation. We find in the Scriptures the saying "How hard it is to kick against the pricks." These are the little pinpricks that annoy us, but we have to put up with them. There are some features to which I would direct the attention of the Minister of Finance and ask for a ruling at the present time. Will merchandise sold prior to May 19, and paid

for but not delivered, be subject to this tax? I understand that the Commissioner of Taxation has ruled that delivery is completion of contract. That ruling was given since this resolution was brought down on May 19. If delivery is completion of contract, then merchandise that has been sold prior to May 19, and paid for but not delivered, would be subject to taxation. I have in mind large timber deals. There are some members of the committee who will understand the working out of that kind of transaction. I understand that it is the custom of lumber dealers to sell their entire cut and get paid for it long before delivery. It is sold very often in the shape of logs in the winter to be manufactured into lumber, and delivered as called for during the ensuing year. Will lumber sold under those conditions be subject to the tax? I have in mind another instance where a manufacturer of grain bags sold for delivery during the months of August, September and October $500,000 worth of grain bags. The orders were put through in the months of January and February, the bags to be delivered at contract price in the months of August, September and October of the same year. Will the manufacturer be obliged to charge his customer the 1 per cent tax on that transaction? If so, I fear there will be a great deal of trouble in 'connection with transactions of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I cannot say that the point raised by the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) has been drawn to my attention before. I would think that the turnover tax is a tax that applies to turnover, and that it would be collected whenever that turn-over takes place. If you have not delivered your goods before the resolutions were brought down, the turn-over tax should be payable. Certainly that is the method by which the converse case would have to be approached. So far as importations are concerned, it does not matter when the goods are sold. It is when they are imported that counts. It seems to me it is the importation on one side and the turnover on the other side which is the thing that counts. As to the point raised as to the manufacturer on the one side and the wholesaler on the other, I confess that our only idea is to try and do the fair thing and not disturb business as it is now being carried on. We are leaving the wholesaler and the manufacturer where they were. It all comes down to this one point. Hon. gentlemen have pointed out that so far as Mie manufacturer is concerned he has to charge 2 per cent, and show it. He must
not include it in his costs, but send it on. So far as the wholesaler is concerned, he has a right to absorb the first one per cent in his costs and charge a profit on it. That statement was made by one hon. gentleman who is objecting from the manufacturer's standpoint. Now it is perfectly obvious that if the wholesaler absorbs that first one per cent in his costs and charges a profit on it, as he can do, his price certainly must be greater than the manufacturer's price, and the manufacturer certainly cannot complain if after he has sold his goods and got the profit he desires to make, the wholesaler absorbs the tax which he has paid to the manufacturer and then puts a profit on top of that again. The manufacturer cannot complain of that kind of competition from the wholesaler.
I do not know that there is anything of real moment in what we are discussing, because after all the whole of this objection is simply this: The manufacturer who is selling direct says: " You make it a little more difficult for me to do business than before, because I have to show a 2 per cent tax, while the wholesaler has only to show a one per cent tax." Now the matter of moment here is that the country gets the benefit of these two turnovers, and the matter of moment further is that there should be some record kept of these taxes; they should be passed along and there should not be too much profit on them. The manufacturer gets none, while the wholesaler can absorb one per cent. It seems to me the fair thing to do would be to treat the manufacturer exactly the same as the wholesaler, and say that in cases where the manufacturer sells direct to the retailer he may absorb one per cent of the 2 per cent, and only show a separate tax of one per cent.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I should just like to suggest to the minister that if in addition to the proposition he has just made, which I think is quite fair, he would give the wholesaler permission, instead of absorbing one per cent, to charge 2 per cent, he would be placing them both on the same footing, and the wholesaler would not be charging a profit on the one per cent. I do not wish to enter into a controversy with my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) as to the advantage of buying from the manufacturer or wholesaler. That is a matter for himself, as a retailer, to consider, as I have no doubt he has been doing for a good many years. I think that if the manufacturer was permitted to absorb one per cent when selling

to the retailer direct, it would overcome a good deal of the difficulty.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I want to say a word nr two in connection with the point raised by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) and the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor). I think this tax is going to work a rather serious injustice on those who have contracted ahead for very large deliveries at a time when this tax could not have been anticipated, because nothing like it has been seen in Canada before. The minister says that this tax is on all-fours with a change in customs duties, but I do not understand that it is. A manufacturer or wholesaler who is selling goods, and who expects the customs duties to be changed, protects himself by saying that should the duty be increased or diminished before the goods are delivered that will be taken into account and the charge will be made accordingly. That is ia common thing in business. It is not a common thing, however, to have an internal tax imposed, and the manufacturers and wholesalers could have no idea that it was coming. Therefore, they are unprotected on their vast commitments for delivery in the autumn of this year. My hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) has given one example, and hundreds of others could be given. I know several firms that have contracted for delivery of 50 or 100 carloads of goods at a certain price without taking this tax into account. That being the case, the whole tax is going to fall on the man who made the contract. And he is going to be compelled to pay not a few dollars but amounts running into thousands of dollars of taxes that he could not foresee, because there has never been anything of this kind before. Therefore it does not stand on all-fours with the customs tax. With regard to binder twine, there is in my riding the largest and only independent binder twine concern in Canada that has survived the benefits of free trade to the binder twine industry. There used to be sixteen or twenty binder twine concerns in Canada before this article was put on the free list, and the number is reduced to one; and as the hon. member for Brant has pointed out, while this institution has to pay a duty of one per cent on about 80 per cent of its raw material-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: On the total cost.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Yes, on the total cost -he is not allowed to make that up as compared with the American, who is exporting this article into Canada entirely free of duty. So that in addition to this product 
being on the free list, the Canadian manufacturer of binder twine will be disadvantaged to a considerable extent on his raw material and all the things that go into the manufacture of binder twine. I do not think the minister wishes to do an injustice of this kind, even if there are only one or two industries of this sort left in Canada. This manufacture of which I speak is a very large institution and is well managed. It has survived the fierce storms of free trade for the last five or ten years, and I trust that the minister will not wipe it out now by exacting a tax on raw materials and subjecting the Canadian manufacturer of this commodity to an impediment which the American manufacturer who ships his goods into Canada will not have to meet. I want to back up my hon. friend (Mr. Harold) in regard to this point because it is a strong one. With regard to the point raised by my hon. friend from Lanark in in connection with the conflict that might arise between the manufacturer and the wholesaler, this is a delicate question and I have been interested in both kinds of business as my hon. friend who is sitting beside me knows. But I want to point out that while it may be good political economy, as the hon. member says, for the manufacturer to go direct to the retailer, that is not always nor nearly always the case. There are certain lines of goods that are in consumption in Canada in every small city, town and village, but it would not pay to send a traveller to any particular section to sell only one line of some goods that might not justify the traveller's expenses. Take scrub brushes for instance, which are handled by every grocer. Now, the brush trade is a big business in itself, but if a manufacturer of brushes were to send a traveller to these outlying districts to take orders which would run from $25 to $50 at the most, the traveller's expenses, salary, etc., would cost the consumers in those little towns and villages more than if the goods were sold to the jobber, who is the wholesaler in this case and who goes all over the country offering one hundred or five hundred lines to one customer. If you split it up to much it becomes not economy but extravagance, and there is no doubt that there are scores of lines, such as brooms, etc., that make up quite a large manufacture in themselves but no one of which is sufficient in volume to pay a traveller to go to distant points. I think therefore that the minister has arrived at a good solution. His proposal is fair and and sound as to the division of the tax, and I trust that the committee will adopt it, be-

cause it is a great advance over what he had in the original resolution.

speechtext: As I recollect the resolution which was read, this 2 per cent or 1 per cent as the case may be, has to be calculated on the value for duty purposes. Now, in regard to goods coming from the continent of Europe, from France, Italy, Austria or Germany, we find that their currencies are so depreciated in comparison with our own that when the Government takes, as it does, the pre-war rate of exchange .as a basis for changing the currencies, when it takes the pre-war rate of exchange for the purpose of changing these invoices into dollars and cents, they raise the value of the goods four and five times; and if the minister takes the value for duty purposes arrived at in this way to fix his tax of two per cent or one per cent, as the case may be, he will be taxing four or five or eight times the amount which under a proper adjustment of the currencies he should tax. I would bring this matter home to the minister because I think that the Customs are making a great mistake in taking a purely arbitrary rate of exchange when they come to levy their duties, a rate which raises the duties to almost a prohibitive extent on things that pay tremendously high duties when they do come in. And then the minister proposes by his amendment to charge the one or two per cent on these inflated and swollen values for duty purposes.

I would ask the minister where the distinction lies between wholesaler and retailer. How is any one to know? I was talking to a large lumber manufacturer in my province no later than yesterday and he was asking me this very question. I could not tell him. I do not suppose that the minister can fully answer every question at a moment's notice, but
the people are deeply interested in these matters and would like to get all the information possible in regard to them. The man to whom I refer put this case to me: A man is the owner of certain timber limits in different sections possibly fifty miles from the owners of the mill who buy the logs. The logs are rolled into the stream fifty miles in the bush, and the mills have their surveyor there to look them over and take control of the logs. The man who owns the timber limits may sell a million feet of lumber to Mr. A, let us say. Is that a wholesale transaction? Mr. A takes them to the stream into the booms and sells them to Mr. B, who in turn sells them and they are manufactured into lumber. There are at least three wholesale transactions in regard to that lumber, and this man to whom I was speaking was anxious to know how those transactions would be regarded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: They would be all wholesale transactions. Transactions of that kind will be defined in the Bill.

speechtext: Has the minister's attention been directed to the question of the cost of containers?
